questions.q: A Class 6 group covers a model of the Earth's surface with 100 equal tiles, blue for water and brown for land. Which split matches the chapter's description of the Earth most closely?
questions.a: About 72 blue and 28 brown
o: About 72 blue and 28 brown
About 82 blue and 18 brown
About 28 blue and 72 brown
About 50 blue and 50 brown

questions.q: True or False? 'Greenland is a landmass even though it is not a continent.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The slip is to treat 'landmass' and 'continent' as the same word. A large body of land is a landmass, but only a large continuous expanse of land is a continent, and the continents do not include all landmass: smaller pieces of land with water on all sides are left out and called islands. Greenland, the largest island, is such a landmass.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: a landmass need not be a continent; continents leave out islands such as Greenland

questions.q:
Read the statements about land and water on the Earth.
1. Every continent is a landmass, but a large body of land need not be a continent.
2. The Southern Hemisphere has more land than the Northern Hemisphere.
3. Seas, bays and gulfs are smaller extensions of the oceans.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: A school paints a globe whose surface measures 1,200 square centimetres. One-fourth of this surface works out to ___ square centimetres, so by the chapter's share of land the brown part should be a little more than that.

Arjun says, 'About three-fourths of the Earth's surface is water, so three-fourths of the Northern Hemisphere and three-fourths of the Southern Hemisphere must each be water.' Test his claim using the chapter.
questions.a: He is wrong. Three-fourths is the share for the whole Earth. The chapter says oceans and continents are not distributed equally between the two hemispheres: the Northern Hemisphere has more land, so its share of water is less than the overall share, and the Southern Hemisphere's share of water is more.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
Three-fourths is an average for the whole surface, not for each half
The Northern Hemisphere has more land (less water), the Southern more water

questions.q:
Match each observation of a photograph of the Earth or a map in Column A with what the chapter says explains it in Column B.
Column A: 1. The Earth looks mostly blue from space  2. White shapes are spread across the globe  3. Brown patches cover only a small part of the picture  4. Blue areas on a map are labelled 'sea', 'bay' or 'gulf'
Column B: a. large masses of clouds  b. smaller extensions of the oceans  c. water covers almost three-fourths of the surface  d. land covers a little over one-fourth of the globe

Correct the two errors in this sentence from a student's notebook: 'The largest bodies of land are called oceans, and bays and gulfs are small pieces of land that jut into them.'
(a) First correction (b) Second correction
questions.a: (a) The oceans are the largest water bodies, not bodies of land (a large continuous expanse of land is a continent). (b) Bays and gulfs are not land: like seas, they are smaller extensions of the oceans, shown in blue.
s: Part (a): oceans are the largest water bodies; large land expanses are continents
Part (b): bays and gulfs are smaller extensions of the oceans, i.e. water

questions.q: A geography club's chart lists Greenland under 'Continents' because it is a large body of land with water on every side. Which reply fits the chapter?
questions.a: It is a landmass, but too small to be a continent: it is an island
o: It is a landmass, but too small to be a continent: it is an island
It is a continent, because every landmass with water around it is one
It is not even a landmass, because it is covered with ice
It counts as part of Europe, so it is listed with that continent

questions.q:
A Class 6 section divides into two groups. Group P estimates land and water on a map of the Earth seen from above one pole, and Group Q does the same for a map seen from above the other pole. Their results (out of 100 equal squares):
Group P: water 61, land 39
Group Q: water 81, land 19
The group labels on the maps have fallen off.
(a) Which group's map shows the Northern Hemisphere? Give the chapter's reason.
(b) Find the average water for the two maps together, and say whether it fits the chapter's description of the whole Earth.
(c) By how many squares is each map's water count above or below 75, the 'three-fourths' mark?
(d) A poster titled 'The Earth is almost three-fourths water' has room for only one of the two maps. Which map misleads less, and what caption must go with it? Use (a) to (c).
questions.a: (a) Group P's map, because the chapter says the Northern Hemisphere has more land, and P counts 39 land squares against Q's 19. (b) (61 + 81) / 2 = 71 water squares, a little under 75, which fits 'almost three-fourths'. (c) P: 75 - 61 = 14 below; Q: 81 - 75 = 6 above. (d) Group Q's map, since its water count is only 6 squares from 75 against 14 for P; the caption must say it shows the Southern Hemisphere, which has more water than the Earth as a whole because the Northern Hemisphere holds more land.
s: Part (a): P's map is the Northern Hemisphere, which has more land
Part (b): average 71, a little under three-fourths, so it fits
Part (c): P is 14 below 75, Q is 6 above
Part (d): Q's map (6 against 14), captioned as the Southern Hemisphere with more water than the whole Earth

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Early astronauts called the Earth the 'blue planet'.
Reason (R): Oceans and continents play a vital role in shaping the climate of the Earth.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
The photograph of the Earth from space is centred on the Indian Ocean. It shows white patches over the open ocean and a large white expanse at the bottom of the globe, over Antarctica.
(a) Should the white expanse at the bottom be counted in the land share or the water share? Give the reason.
(b) Should the white patches over the open ocean be counted as land? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) The land share: the white expanse is Antarctica, a continent that is mostly ice, so it is land. (b) No: those white shapes are large masses of clouds, not land, so they add nothing to the land share.
s: Part (a): land, because it is Antarctica, an ice-covered continent
Part (b): no, the white patches are masses of clouds

questions.q: While estimating land and water on a map, a student counts the Arabian Sea, the Bay of Bengal and every gulf as land 'because they are not called oceans'. What happens to her result?
questions.a: Her land share comes out too large, as seas, bays and gulfs belong to the oceans
o: Her land share comes out too large, as seas, bays and gulfs belong to the oceans
Her result is unchanged, as seas, bays and gulfs are too small to matter
Her water share comes out too large, as seas are counted twice on maps
Her land share comes out too small, as seas, bays and gulfs count as water twice

questions.q: Nikhil says, 'A large body of land and a continent mean the same thing.' (a) Give the chapter's meaning of each term. (b) Use Europe and Asia to show how the two terms can give different counts for the same land.
questions.a: (a) A large body of land is a landmass; a large continuous expanse of land is a continent. (b) The map shows Europe and Asia as a single landmass, yet they are generally counted as two continents, so one landmass can be two continents and the terms are not the same.
s: Part (a): landmass is a large body of land; continent a large continuous expanse
Part (b): Europe and Asia are one landmass but generally two continents

questions.q:
Jules Verne wrote in 1870 that the ocean 'covers seven-tenths of the terrestrial globe'. The chapter says water covers almost three-fourths of the Earth's surface.
(a) Write both figures as parts out of 100.
(b) By how many parts do they differ?
(c) Does Verne's figure contradict the chapter? Judge, giving a reason.
questions.a: (a) Verne: 70 parts; the chapter: almost 75 parts. (b) About 5 parts out of 100, a little less because 'almost' three-fourths is a bit under 75. (c) No real contradiction: both say most of the surface (well over half) is water; Verne's figure is only a little lower than the chapter's.
s: Part (a): 70 and almost 75
Part (b): about 5 parts
Part (c): no contradiction, both say most of the surface is water; Verne's is a little lower

questions.q: A student looks at the photograph of the Earth centred on the Indian Ocean. She sees Africa, Asia, Australia and Antarctica and says, 'Four big pieces of land, so the Earth must be mostly land.' What is wrong with her reasoning?
questions.a: The number of landmasses says nothing about how much area they cover
o: The number of landmasses says nothing about how much area they cover
Antarctica is ice, so it does not count as part of the Earth
The photograph shows only the Southern Hemisphere
Clouds hide most of the oceans, so very little blue can be seen in it

questions.q: Write three clues for a quiz whose answer is 'the blue planet'. Each clue must use a different fact from the chapter, and none may contain the word 'blue'.
questions.a: For example: 1. Early astronauts gave me this loving name. 2. Almost three-fourths of my surface is covered with water. 3. Seen from outer space, my oceans are the most widespread colour you notice. (Any three correct, different chapter facts, without the word 'blue'.)
s: First clue uses a correct chapter fact
Second clue uses a different correct fact
Third clue uses a third fact and no clue says 'blue'

questions.q: 'One photograph of the Earth taken from space cannot tell the whole story of its land and water.' Justify this statement using the chapter. Cover: what the blue and the brown stand for and how much of the surface each covers; what the white areas are; what blue areas besides the oceans show; and why maps seen from above both poles are needed.
questions.a: Blue is water: almost three-fourths of the surface, which is why the Earth looks mostly blue and was called the blue planet. Brown is land, a little over one-fourth of the globe. White shapes are large masses of clouds, while the white expanse at the bottom is Antarctica, mostly ice, which is land; so white cannot simply be read as land or water. Blue also includes the smaller extensions of the oceans, the seas, bays and gulfs. A single photograph shows one side only; the maps seen from above the North Pole and the South Pole show that land and water are not distributed equally and that the Northern Hemisphere has more land. So the full story needs the shares, the meaning of each colour and both hemispheres.
s: Blue water, almost three-fourths; the blue planet
Brown land, a little over one-fourth
White: clouds, and Antarctica's ice which is land
Seas, bays and gulfs are part of the blue
Maps above both poles show the Northern Hemisphere has more land

questions.q:
A geography club is making a card game. Each card describes a piece of land:
Card 1: Europe and Asia together; the map shows no sea dividing them.
Card 2: Greenland; water on all sides; smaller than any continent.
Card 3: Australia; water on all sides; very large.
Card 4: India's Andaman and Nicobar Islands in the Bay of Bengal.
The club must sort the cards into two boxes, 'Continent' and 'Not a continent'.
(a) Which of the four cards describe a landmass?
(b) Why is Card 3 a continent although, like Card 2, it has water on all sides?
(c) How many continents does Card 1 stand for in the seven-continent count, and how many in the geologists' view?
(d) Into which box should Card 1 go, and why does the choice of count not change the box?
questions.a: (a) All four describe land. Cards 1 to 3 are large bodies of land, so landmasses; Card 4 is a group of the smaller pieces of land that the book says are left out of the continents and called islands. (b) Continents are also surrounded by water, but they are so large that they are not considered islands; Greenland is a smaller piece left out of the continents. (c) Two (Europe and Asia) in the seven-continent count; one, Eurasia, for geologists. (d) 'Continent': whether it is counted as two continents or as the single continent Eurasia, the land on Card 1 is continent land in every count.
s: Part (a): all four are land; Cards 1-3 large landmasses, Card 4 islands left out of the continents
Part (b): continents are too large to be called islands
Part (c): two in the seven count, one (Eurasia) for geologists
Part (d): 'Continent' box, since it is continent land under either count

questions.q:
Compare the Northern and Southern Hemispheres as the chapter presents them, and analyse what the two maps seen from above the poles teach us.
(a) What does each map show, and which hemisphere has more land?
(b) Why is the Earth's share of water (almost three-fourths) not the same as each hemisphere's share?
(c) Which blue areas besides the oceans appear on such maps?
(d) A classmate looks only at the map seen from above the North Pole and says the whole Earth has the same share of land as that map. Use (a) and (b) to show his error.
questions.a: (a) One map shows the Earth from above the North Pole, the other from above the South Pole; the Northern Hemisphere shows more land. (b) Almost three-fourths is the average for the whole surface; because land is not distributed equally, the Northern Hemisphere has less than that share of water and the Southern more. (c) Smaller extensions of the oceans: seas, bays and gulfs. (d) That map shows only the Northern Hemisphere, which has more land than the Southern; the whole Earth has a little over one-fourth land, a smaller share than the Northern map shows.
s: Part (a): the two polar views; the Northern Hemisphere has more land
Part (b): three-fourths is a whole-Earth average, shares differ by hemisphere
Part (c): seas, bays and gulfs
Part (d): one hemisphere is not the whole Earth; the Earth's land is a little over one-fourth, less than the Northern map shows

questions.q:
A map of the Indian coast shows the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal in blue.
(a) What are a sea and a bay, according to the chapter?
(b) Should their area be counted in the Earth's water share of almost three-fourths? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) They are smaller extensions of the oceans. (b) Yes: they are parts of the oceans, shown in blue with them, so they belong to the Earth's water share.
s: Part (a): smaller extensions of the oceans
Part (b): yes, they are part of the ocean water

questions.q: A spacecraft photographs a planet that looks about one-fourth blue and three-fourths brown. Reading the colours as the chapter does for the Earth, how does this planet compare with the Earth?
questions.a: Its shares of water and land are the reverse of the Earth's
o: Its shares of water and land are the reverse of the Earth's
Its shares of water and land are the same as the Earth's
It has an even larger share of water than the Earth, as blue always means oceans
It has equal shares of water and land, unlike the Earth

questions.q:
A photograph of the Earth taken from space is described in words. A very large ocean fills the centre. A continent lies to its left, a continent with a land jutting southwards into the water lies at the top, a smaller continent lies to the right, and a white, mostly icy continent lies at the bottom. The continent on the left marks the west.
(a) Which ocean fills the centre? Use the land around it to decide.
(b) Which ocean lies between the centre ocean and the icy continent at the bottom?
(c) Name the two parts of the centre ocean that lie on either side of the land jutting southwards at the top (India), and say which lies on which side.
(d) Riya needs a picture for a project on the sea to the west of India. A friend says this photograph is no use because it is centred on the open ocean. Can Riya use it, and on which side of India, left or right, should she point? Justify using (a) and (c).
questions.a: (a) The Indian Ocean: it has Africa to the west (left), Asia to the north (top) and Australia to the east (right). (b) The Southern Ocean, the Indian Ocean's limit in the south. (c) The Arabian Sea to the west of India and the Bay of Bengal to the east. (d) Yes: the Arabian Sea is a part of the Indian Ocean, which fills this photograph, and since the left of this view is west, she should point to the left of India.
s: Part (a): the Indian Ocean, from Africa west, Asia north, Australia east
Part (b): the Southern Ocean
Part (c): Arabian Sea west, Bay of Bengal east
Part (d): yes, the Arabian Sea is in the photo, to the left (west) of India

questions.q: A boat leaves a port on the Bay of Bengal, sails round the southern tip of India and then north along India's western coast. Where is it now, and has it left the ocean it started in?
questions.a: In the Arabian Sea, still within the Indian Ocean
o: In the Arabian Sea, still within the Indian Ocean
In the Arabian Sea, which lies in the Atlantic Ocean
Still in the Bay of Bengal, which wraps round India
In the Southern Ocean, after leaving the Indian Ocean

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal are both parts of the same ocean.
Reason (R): The Arabian Sea lies to the east of India and the Bay of Bengal to the west.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: True or False? 'The world map draws lines between the five oceans, so a body of seawater in the Indian Ocean stays in the Indian Ocean.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the lines dividing the oceans are no more than conventions; seawater constantly flows across different oceans.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: the lines are conventions and seawater flows across oceans

questions.q: A student ranks the oceans from largest to smallest as: Pacific, Indian, Atlantic, Southern, Arctic. What single change makes her list match the chapter?
questions.a: Swap the Indian and the Atlantic
o: Swap the Indian and the Atlantic
Swap the Southern and the Arctic
Swap the Pacific and the Atlantic
Swap the Indian and the Southern

questions.q: Kiran says, 'The Indian Ocean is closed in by land on every side: Asia, Africa and Australia.' How far is she right? Use the chapter's limits of the Indian Ocean.
questions.a: Partly right. Asia to the north, Africa to the west and Australia to the east are indeed its main limits. But the south is not land: the Indian Ocean is limited there by the Southern Ocean, so it is not closed in on every side.
s: Verdict: partly right
Correct part: Asia north, Africa west, Australia east
Wrong part: the southern limit is the Southern Ocean, not land

questions.q:
A ship starts in the middle of the Indian Ocean and sails in one direction until it meets the first limit of the Indian Ocean named in the chapter. Match the direction in Column A with what the ship meets in Column B.
Column A: 1. North  2. West  3. East  4. South
Column B: a. Africa  b. the Southern Ocean  c. Asia  d. Australia

A diver's log lists: algae, seaweeds, dolphins and whales.
(a) Sort the four into marine flora and marine fauna.
(b) Her friend writes, 'Marine fauna means the animals of any region.' Correct him using the meanings of both words.
questions.a: (a) Flora: algae and seaweeds; fauna: dolphins and whales. (b) Fauna alone means the animal life of a particular region; 'marine' means related to or found in the oceans and seas, so marine fauna is the animal life of the oceans and seas, not of any region.
s: Part (a): algae and seaweeds flora; dolphins and whales fauna
Part (b): marine means of the oceans and seas, so marine fauna is ocean animal life only

questions.q:
A ship's log records a voyage in four legs.
Leg 1: from a port on India's western coast, out into the sea beside it.
Leg 2: westwards across the open ocean until the coast of the continent that limits this ocean in the west.
Leg 3: southwards until the ocean around the icy southern continent.
Leg 4: back north-east, round India's southern tip, ending in the sea on India's eastern side.
(a) Name the sea, continent or ocean at the end of each leg, using the chapter.
(b) In how many different oceans did the ship sail, and should the log record crossing any real boundary between them? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Leg 1: the Arabian Sea (west of India). Leg 2: Africa, the Indian Ocean's western limit. Leg 3: the Southern (Antarctic) Ocean, the Indian Ocean's southern limit. Leg 4: the Bay of Bengal, east of India. (b) Two: the Indian Ocean (with its parts, the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal) and the Southern Ocean. No real boundary was crossed: the lines dividing oceans on a map are only conventions, and seawater flows across them.
s: Leg 1: the Arabian Sea
Leg 2: Africa
Leg 3: the Southern (Antarctic) Ocean
Leg 4: the Bay of Bengal
Part (b): two oceans; the dividing line is only a convention

questions.q: A quiz card lists the five oceans from the SMALLEST to the LARGEST, starting with position 1. The Atlantic Ocean is in position ___.

On a class map, Asha labels the ocean around the icy continent at the bottom of the globe 'Antarctic Ocean'; Dev crosses it out and writes 'Southern Ocean'.
(a) Was Asha's label wrong? Explain using the chapter.
(b) Asha then counts 'Antarctic Ocean' and 'Southern Ocean' as two different oceans in her list. With the other four oceans also in her list, how many oceans does it now show, and what is wrong with it?
questions.a: (a) No. The chapter calls it the Southern (or Antarctic) Ocean, so both names are correct. (b) Six instead of the chapter's five: the two names belong to one ocean, so she has counted the same ocean twice.
s: Part (a): both names are used for the same ocean
Part (b): six, because one ocean is counted twice under two names

questions.q: A student's chart of where the Earth's water is held shows rivers and lakes as the biggest share, because 'that is where people take water from'. Which fact from the chapter corrects her chart?
questions.a: The oceans together hold most of the water on the planet
o: The oceans together hold most of the water on the planet
Rivers and lakes hold half the water, the oceans the rest
The clouds in the atmosphere hold most of the water
The Pacific alone holds more water than all land put together

questions.q: A museum must choose one label for its world-ocean gallery: 'Five separate oceans' or 'One connected ocean with five names'. Interpret which label fits the chapter better, giving three facts from the chapter.
questions.a: 'One connected ocean with five names'. The world map does list five oceans, so the names are real; but the lines that divide them are no more than conventions, as the natural world does not follow such boundaries; and seawater constantly flows across the oceans, so many plant and animal species are found in more than one ocean.
s: Five oceans are named on the map
The dividing lines are only conventions
Seawater flows across and species live in several oceans, so the connected label fits

questions.q:
Read the statements about the oceans.
1. The Arctic Ocean is the fourth largest ocean.
2. The Southern Ocean is also called the Antarctic Ocean.
3. Seawater constantly flows across different oceans.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Map X shows the Bay of Bengal to the west of India and the Arabian Sea to the east; Map Y shows them the other way round.
(a) Which map is correct?
(b) Using the correct map, which of the two seas would a ship enter first if it sailed from Mumbai towards the continent that limits the Indian Ocean in the west? Name that continent.
questions.a: (a) Map Y: the Arabian Sea is to the west of India and the Bay of Bengal to the east. (b) The Arabian Sea, because it lies on India's western side, towards Africa, which limits the Indian Ocean in the west.
s: Part (a): Map Y, Arabian Sea west and Bay of Bengal east
Part (b): the Arabian Sea, on the way west to Africa

questions.q:
A school geography club is making a large wall map of the oceans for a quiz on their names. Team A wants each ocean filled with its own bright colour, edged with a thick solid line, and its name printed in large lettering, so that juniors can tell the five apart at a glance. Team B wants one shade of blue for all the water, with thin dotted lines, each marked 'boundary drawn by people', and the names in small print.
(a) What does the chapter say about the lines that divide the oceans on a map?
(b) Give one fact about seawater that supports this.
(c) Give one fact about living things that supports it.
(d) Team A's map is clearer; Team B's is closer to the chapter. Which design should the club choose, and which one of Team A's three features could it borrow without going against (a) to (c)? Justify.
questions.a: (a) They are no more than conventions; the natural world does not follow such boundaries. (b) Seawater constantly flows across different oceans. (c) Many plant and animal species are found across multiple oceans. (d) Team B's design, because thick solid lines and separate colours would teach that the oceans are separate, which (a) to (c) show they are not. It can borrow Team A's large lettering for the names: bigger names help juniors tell the five oceans apart without suggesting any wall between them.
s: Part (a): the dividing lines are only conventions
Part (b): seawater flows across the oceans
Part (c): many species live across several oceans
Part (d): Team B's design, borrowing Team A's large lettering (not the colours or solid lines)

questions.q:
Two divers compare logs. One dived near the sun-lit surface, the other went down into the dark depths; their lists share almost none of the same creatures.
(a) Which idea from the chapter explains why the lists differ?
(b) Seawater flows across oceans, and many species are found in several oceans. Does that mean the same creatures should live at every depth? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Each part of the ocean, from the sun-lit surface to the dark depths, has its own diverse life forms. (b) No: the flow of seawater lets species be found across several oceans, but within an ocean each depth still has its own life forms, so the surface and the depths hold different creatures.
s: Part (a): each part, surface to depths, has its own life forms
Part (b): no, spreading across oceans is different from living at every depth

questions.q:
A corridor chart in a school says:
1. The Atlantic is the largest ocean on Earth.
2. The Arctic Ocean is the fourth largest.
3. The Bay of Bengal lies to the west of India.
4. Australia limits the Indian Ocean on the west.
5. Solid boundaries keep each ocean's water and sea life apart.
Identify the error in each line and correct it using the chapter.
questions.a: 1. The Pacific is the largest; the Atlantic is second. 2. The Southern Ocean is the fourth largest; the Arctic is the smallest. 3. The Bay of Bengal is east of India; the Arabian Sea is west. 4. Africa limits it on the west; Australia is on the east. 5. The boundaries are only conventions: seawater flows across oceans and many species are found in several oceans.
s: Line 1: the Pacific is largest, Atlantic second
Line 2: the Southern Ocean is fourth, the Arctic smallest
Line 3: the Bay of Bengal is east of India
Line 4: Africa is the western limit, Australia the eastern
Line 5: boundaries are conventions; water and species cross them

questions.q: The answer to a quiz question is 'the Bay of Bengal'. Write a question about position (using directions from India and the ocean it belongs to) for which this is the ONLY correct answer, and explain why the Arabian Sea does not fit it.
questions.a: For example: 'Which part of the Indian Ocean lies to the east of India?' Only the Bay of Bengal lies east of India within the Indian Ocean. The Arabian Sea does not fit because it lies to the west of India.
s: A question naming east of India and the Indian Ocean
Shows the Bay of Bengal is the only part east of India
Arabian Sea excluded because it is west of India

questions.q: A student ranks the five oceans from largest to smallest as: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Arctic, Southern. Which single correction makes her list match the chapter?
questions.a: Swap the last two: the Southern Ocean is fourth, the Arctic smallest
o: Swap the last two: the Southern Ocean is fourth, the Arctic smallest
Swap the first two: the Atlantic is the largest and the Pacific second
Move the Indian Ocean up above the Atlantic, into second place on the list
Make no change, since her list already matches the chapter

questions.q: A farmer in Maharashtra says, 'If the clouds stopped coming in from the ocean, our fields would suffer, not just the fishermen's boats.' Is the farmer right? Use the chapter.
questions.a: Yes. The chapter says the monsoon rains India expects every summer originate in the ocean, brought by clouds to the continents, and that without such rains agriculture and all life would suffer. So farmers inland depend on the ocean too.
s: Verdict: right
Monsoon rains originate in the ocean and are brought by clouds
Without them agriculture and all life would suffer

questions.q: Two news reports: (1) Sensors pick up a strong undersea earthquake, and coasts in several countries around the Indian Ocean are alerted before any wave arrives. (2) After a cyclone floods a coastal district, India's own authority for all kinds of disasters takes charge of the response. Which pair names the arrangement in (1) and then the body in (2)?
questions.a: The Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning System, then the National Disaster Management Authority
o: The Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning System, then the National Disaster Management Authority
The National Disaster Management Authority, then the Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning System
The Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning System, then the Indian Antarctica Programme
The National Disaster Management Authority, then the United Nations World Oceans Day

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A tsunami can cause damage on coasts far away from where it began.
Reason (R): Tsunamis can travel thousands of kilometres.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: True or False? 'The same ocean that brings India its monsoon rains can also bring disaster to India's coasts.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The monsoon rains originate in the ocean, but oceans also give rise to cyclones that damage coastal regions and to tsunamis that submerge coastal areas.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: rains come from the ocean, and so do cyclones and tsunamis

questions.q:
Match each news headline in Column A with the term from the chapter in Column B.
Column A: 1. 'Clouds roll in from the sea; rains reach the farms at last'  2. 'Two days of very strong winds and extreme rain batter the coast'  3. 'Giant wave floods coastline after quake beneath the sea'  4. 'Countries share data; wave spotted hours before it reaches land'
Column B: a. tsunami  b. monsoon  c. early warning system  d. cyclone

A district disaster cell on India's coast has one evacuation team. On the same morning it receives two alerts.
Alert 1 (ocean warning centre): a strong earthquake has struck the sea floor far away; a huge wave may reach the beach villages in about 5 hours. Moving the beach villages takes the team 4 hours.
Alert 2 (weather office): a violent storm with very strong winds and extreme rain will reach the coast in about 22 hours. Moving the families in its path takes the team 20 hours.
(a) Name the disaster each alert describes, with one clue from each alert.
(b) If the team moves the storm families first, when does it finish, and is that before the wave arrives?
(c) If it moves the beach villages first and then the storm families, when does it finish, and by how many hours does it miss the storm?
(d) Which order should the cell choose, and what else must it do? Justify using (b) and (c).
questions.a: (a) Alert 1: a tsunami, a huge wave caused by an earthquake at the bottom of the ocean. Alert 2: a cyclone, a storm with very strong winds and extreme rainfall. (b) After 20 hours, long after the wave arrives at about 5 hours, so the beach villages would not be moved in time. (c) 4 + 20 = 24 hours, which is 24 - 22 = 2 hours after the storm arrives. (d) Beach villages first: that order saves everyone in the tsunami's path and leaves only a 2-hour shortfall for the cyclone, while the other order leaves the beach villages unprotected; the cell must also ask for more help (disaster management, such as the National Disaster Management Authority) to close the 2-hour gap.
s: Part (a): tsunami (undersea quake, huge wave) and cyclone (strong winds, extreme rain)
Part (b): 20 hours, after the 5-hour wave, so too late
Part (c): 24 hours, 2 hours after the storm
Part (d): beach villages first, and call for extra help for the 2-hour gap

questions.q: A strong earthquake shakes the ocean floor 2,400 km away from a fishing town. A resident says, 'A wave cannot come from that far.' The chapter answers him: tsunamis can travel ___ of kilometres and submerge coastal areas.
questions.a: thousands

questions.q:
A coastal warning room receives two reports at once.
Report 1: a strong volcanic eruption at the bottom of the ocean.
Report 2: a cyclone forming over the sea, with very strong winds.
(a) Which report should trigger a tsunami alert? Give the chapter's reason.
(b) Why should the other report still not be ignored by coastal districts?
questions.a: (a) Report 1: the chapter says a tsunami is generally caused by a strong earthquake or a volcanic eruption at the bottom of the ocean; a cyclone is not one of these causes. (b) A cyclone is a storm with extreme rainfall or very strong winds, which can itself cause widespread damage to coastal regions.
s: Part (a): Report 1, since an undersea volcanic eruption (or strong earthquake) generally causes a tsunami
Part (b): cyclones are violent storms that damage coastal regions

questions.q: A coast floods under a wall of water on a calm, clear day with no wind, one hour after a strong earthquake beneath the ocean. Which description fits the chapter?
questions.a: A tsunami, a huge wave caused by the undersea quake
o: A tsunami, a huge wave caused by the undersea quake
A cyclone, a violent storm with very strong winds and rain
Monsoon rain, carried from the ocean by clouds
Heavy rain from clouds that formed over the ocean

questions.q:
Read the statements about the tsunami of 26 December 2004.
1. It struck India and 13 other countries around the Indian Ocean.
2. It was caused by an earthquake in Indonesia.
3. In India, the worst-hit areas were the Lakshadweep Islands and the coast of Gujarat.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
A class lists three events from one year: a cyclone that destroys houses on one coast, a tsunami that takes lives on another, and a heavy shower that floods no home and harms no one.
(a) Which of the three come under 'disaster management' by the chapter's meaning? Give the test you used.
(b) Which Indian body deals with them, and is it meant only for disasters from the ocean?
questions.a: (a) The cyclone and the tsunami: disaster management handles events that lead to loss of life and property, and the shower caused neither. (b) The National Disaster Management Authority; no, it deals with all kinds of disasters, not only those from the ocean.
s: Part (a): cyclone and tsunami, by the test of loss of life and property
Part (b): the NDMA, which deals with all kinds of disasters

questions.q: Differentiate between the Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning System and India's National Disaster Management Authority: who runs each, and what is each for?
questions.a: The Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning System is a shared effort to which many countries, including India, contribute; it detects tsunamis before they hit a coast so that measures can be taken. The National Disaster Management Authority is India's own body that deals with all kinds of disasters.
s: Warning System: many countries together, early detection of tsunamis
NDMA: India's own body for all kinds of disasters

questions.q: Show that a coastal village cannot rely on watching the sky for storm clouds to get a warning of a tsunami.
questions.a: A tsunami is generally caused by a strong earthquake or a volcanic eruption at the bottom of the ocean, not by a storm in the sky. It can travel thousands of kilometres, so it can strike a coast far from where it began. That is why tsunamis are detected by early warning systems, such as the Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning System, which help people take measures in time.
s: Cause is an undersea earthquake or eruption, not a storm
It travels thousands of kilometres from where it began
So warning comes from early warning systems

questions.q:
A student says, 'Tsunamis are rare, so preparing for them is a waste of effort.'
(a) Weigh 'rare' against what the chapter says about how far a tsunami can travel and what it does to coasts.
(b) How does early warning make preparation worthwhile?
questions.a: (a) Tsunamis are rare but very destructive: they can travel thousands of kilometres, so even a faraway undersea earthquake can reach a coast, and they submerge coastal areas, causing widespread damage. Rarity does not lower the damage when one comes. (b) They can often be detected before they hit a coast, which helps people take measures to protect lives and property.
s: Part (a): rare but very destructive; travel thousands of km and submerge coasts
Part (b): early detection allows measures to protect lives and property

questions.q: A family must choose between two houses: one on the sea coast and one in a town far inland. Compare the ocean-related dangers and benefits each house would have, using the chapter.
questions.a: Coast: open to cyclones, which cause widespread damage to coastal regions, and to tsunamis, which submerge coastal areas. Inland: safe from these direct coastal dangers. Both houses depend on the ocean for the monsoon rains, which originate in the ocean; without them agriculture and all life would suffer.
s: Coast faces cyclones that damage coastal regions
Coast faces tsunamis that submerge coastal areas; inland is spared these
Both depend on monsoon rains that come from the ocean

questions.q: The same tsunami strikes two coastal towns. Town A was alerted three hours earlier through the Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning System; Town B received no warning. Which outcome does the chapter's account lead us to expect?
questions.a: Town A could take measures to protect lives and property, so its losses would be smaller
o: Town A could take measures to protect lives and property, so its losses would be smaller
Town A would escape the wave entirely, because the warning stops the wave out at sea
Both towns would suffer the same losses, because a tsunami cannot be detected in advance
Town B would suffer less, because only towns that receive warnings are struck by the wave

questions.q: 'For India, the ocean is both a giver and a destroyer.' Justify this statement using the chapter. Include what the ocean gives, two kinds of disaster it causes, why one of them can strike far from where it begins, and how India reduces the damage.
questions.a: Giver: the clouds over the ocean bring the monsoon rains India expects every summer; without them agriculture and all life would suffer. Destroyer: cyclones, violent storms with extreme rainfall or very strong winds, damage coastal regions; tsunamis, huge waves generally caused by undersea earthquakes or volcanic eruptions, submerge coasts. Far-reaching: tsunamis can travel thousands of kilometres, so a quake far away can still hit India's coast. Reducing damage: tsunamis can often be detected early through the Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning System, to which India contributes, and the National Disaster Management Authority deals with all kinds of disasters.
s: Giver: monsoon rains from the ocean sustain farming and life
Destroyer: cyclones damage coastal regions
Destroyer: tsunamis from undersea quakes or eruptions submerge coasts
Tsunamis travel thousands of kilometres, so a distant quake can hit India
Reducing damage: the warning system and the NDMA

questions.q:
A memorial stone in a coastal village of Tamil Nadu reads:
'Here we remember those we lost when the sea rose without warning on 26 December 2004. Such a sea can never be seen coming.'
A student visiting it in 2026 learns that the earthquake behind it struck near Indonesia, far from Tamil Nadu.
(a) What kind of disaster was it, and what generally causes such a disaster?
(b) Which property of this disaster explains how a quake so far away could reach this village?
(c) In how many countries in all were people struck that day, and about how many lives were lost? Was the village's loss a local event or part of a wider disaster?
(d) Is the last line of the stone still true today? Justify using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) A tsunami, a huge and powerful wave generally caused by a strong earthquake or a volcanic eruption at the bottom of the ocean. (b) Tsunamis can travel thousands of kilometres and submerge coastal areas. (c) 14 countries (India and 13 others) around the Indian Ocean, with more than two lakh lives lost, so it was part of a much wider disaster. (d) No: tsunamis are rare but can often be detected before they hit a coast, and the Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning System, to which India contributes, helps people take measures in time.
s: Part (a): a tsunami, caused by an undersea earthquake or volcanic eruption
Part (b): tsunamis travel thousands of kilometres
Part (c): 14 countries, more than two lakh lives; a wider disaster
Part (d): no, early warning systems can often detect tsunamis

questions.q:
Compare a cyclone and a tsunami under these heads, and analyse which of the two an early warning system mentioned in the chapter is built for.
(a) Where each begins and what causes or makes it up
(b) What kind of event each is
(c) Which areas each damages
(d) Which of the two the chapter calls rare but very destructive
(e) The warning system and the authority that help
questions.a: (a) Both begin in the ocean; a cyclone is a storm, while a tsunami is generally caused by a strong earthquake or a volcanic eruption at the ocean bottom. (b) A cyclone is a violent event with extreme rainfall or very strong winds; a tsunami is a huge, powerful wave that can travel thousands of kilometres. (c) Both damage coastal regions; tsunamis submerge coastal areas. (d) The tsunami: the chapter says such tsunamis are rare but very destructive. (e) The Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning System is built for tsunamis; the National Disaster Management Authority deals with all kinds of disasters, including both.
s: Part (a): both oceanic; tsunami from undersea quake or eruption
Part (b): storm with rain and wind versus a huge travelling wave
Part (c): both hit coastal regions
Part (d): the tsunami is the rare but very destructive one
Part (e): warning system for tsunamis; NDMA for all disasters

questions.q:
Here is the answer to an exam question: 'Because it begins in the ocean, can travel thousands of kilometres and strikes coastal areas.'
(a) Write a question about tsunamis for which this is the answer.
(b) Which parts of the answer would also fit a cyclone, and which part does the chapter say only about tsunamis?
questions.a: (a) For example: 'Why can a tsunami cause damage on coasts far from where it starts?' (b) A cyclone also begins in the ocean and damages coastal regions; only for tsunamis does the chapter say they travel thousands of kilometres.
s: Part (a): a fitting question about tsunamis
Part (b): ocean origin and coastal damage also fit a cyclone
Part (b): travelling thousands of kilometres is said only of tsunamis

questions.q: Why does India contribute to a tsunami warning system shared with many countries, instead of only watching its own coast?
questions.a: A tsunami can travel thousands of km, so its cause may lie far away
o: A tsunami can travel thousands of km, so its cause may lie far away
Tsunamis start only near India, so other countries need India's data
Each country can stop a tsunami once it reaches its own coastline
Cyclones and tsunamis are the same, so one shared forecast serves all

questions.q: An old atlas lists the continents as: Africa-Eurasia, America, Antarctica, Australia. Compared with the most widely used list, what has it done?
questions.a: Made three joins, giving four continents
o: Made three joins, giving four continents
Made two joins, giving five continents
Made three joins, giving five continents
Made four joins, giving three continents

questions.q: A map-maker starts from the seven-continent list, then joins Europe with Asia and North America with South America. Her new list has ___ continents.

Read a traveller's blog post.
'On my world trip I visited Kenya in Africa, France in Europe, Japan in Asia, Brazil in South America, Canada in North America, and Australia. The only continent I have never set foot on is the frozen one at the bottom of the globe.'
(a) Using the seven-continent count, which continent has she missed, and how many has she visited?
(b) Using the four-continent count, how many of the four has she visited? Name them.
(c) Using the five-continent count, how many of the five has she visited?
(d) Her friend says, 'Whichever count you use, you have missed exactly one continent.' Is the friend right? Justify from your answers.
questions.a: (a) Antarctica; she has visited 6 of 7. (b) 3 of 4: Africa-Eurasia (Kenya, France, Japan), America (Brazil, Canada) and Australia. (c) 4 of 5: Africa, Eurasia, America and Australia. (d) Yes. Every count in the chapter includes Antarctica as one continent, and every other continent in each count holds a place she visited, so she misses exactly one each time (also 5 of 6 in the six-continent count).
s: Part (a): Antarctica; 6 of 7
Part (b): 3 of 4 (Africa-Eurasia, America, Australia)
Part (c): 4 of 5
Part (d): yes, Antarctica is in every count and she misses only it

questions.q:

Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true.
o: A is false, but R is true.
A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.q:
Atlas A in a library says there are seven continents; Atlas B says there are five.
(a) Can both atlases be correct? Explain using the chapter.
(b) Which two pairs of continents has Atlas B joined?
questions.a: (a) Yes. The chapter says continents can be counted in several ways, anywhere from four to seven, depending on how adjoining landmasses are grouped. (b) Europe with Asia (as Eurasia), and North America with South America (as America).
s: Part (a): yes, the count depends on how landmasses are grouped
Part (b): Europe-Asia as Eurasia and the two Americas as America

questions.q:
Match each count of continents in Column A with its list in Column B.

questions.q: True or False? 'Africa and Eurasia are generally counted as one continent, which is why the four-continent list is the one most widely used.' Give the verdict and the correction.
questions.a: False. Africa and Eurasia are generally regarded as two continents and only sometimes as one; the list most widely adopted and used is the seven-continent list, not the four-continent one.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: generally two, sometimes one; seven is the most widely used count

questions.q:
Read the statements about the counts of continents.

questions.q:

(a) How many continents does the photograph show under the seven-continent count?
(b) How many under the four-continent count? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Four: Africa, Asia, Australia and Antarctica. (b) Three: the four-continent count joins Asia (inside Eurasia) with Africa as Africa-Eurasia, leaving Africa-Eurasia, Australia and Antarctica.
s: Part (a): four
Part (b): three, as Africa and Asia fall in one continent, Africa-Eurasia

questions.q:
The photograph of the Earth at the start of the chapter shows 'India and part of Asia at the top'.
(a) In the seven-continent count, which continent is India part of?
(b) Which continent would India be part of in the four-continent count? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Asia. (b) Africa-Eurasia, because the four-continent count joins Europe and Asia into Eurasia and then joins Africa with Eurasia.
s: Part (a): Asia
Part (b): Africa-Eurasia, as Asia is inside Eurasia which is joined with Africa

questions.q:
(a) In which of the chapter's counts is South America a continent on its own?
(b) Why do the four- and five-continent counts not treat it so?
questions.a: (a) In the six- and seven-continent counts. (b) They see North America and South America as a single landmass and count it as one continent, America.
s: Part (a): six and seven
Part (b): the two Americas are joined as one landmass, America

questions.q: Rohit says, 'The number of continents is a fixed fact of nature, just as the five oceans are five separate things in nature.' Test both halves of his claim using the chapter.
questions.a: He is wrong on both halves. The continents can be counted anywhere from four to seven, depending on whether adjoining landmasses are counted as one or two, so the number is a matter of choice. The oceans, too, are not really separate: the lines dividing them are conventions, and seawater flows across them.
s: Verdict: wrong
Continent count is a choice, four to seven
Oceans are not separate; their boundaries are conventions

questions.q: Show that a list of continents cannot correctly contain both 'Eurasia' and 'Europe'.
questions.a: Eurasia is the name for Europe and Asia taken together as the single landmass they form. Europe is therefore already inside Eurasia. Listing both would count Europe twice, so no count in the chapter does it (the six- and five-continent lists have Eurasia only, the seven-continent list has Europe and Asia only).
s: Eurasia means Europe and Asia together
Europe is already part of it, so it would be counted twice
The chapter's lists use either Eurasia or Europe and Asia, never both

questions.q: Four classmates copy the chapter's counts of continents into their notebooks. One of them copies a list that is NOT any of the chapter's counts. Which list is it?
questions.a: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, America
o: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, America
Africa, Antarctica, Australia, Eurasia, North America, South America
Africa, America, Antarctica, Australia, Eurasia
Africa-Eurasia, America, Antarctica, Australia

questions.q: Write step-by-step instructions that turn the seven-continent list into the four-continent list, one join per step, and state how many joins you made.
questions.a: Step 1: join Europe and Asia into Eurasia (six continents). Step 2: join North America and South America into America (five). Step 3: join Africa and Eurasia into Africa-Eurasia (four). Three joins in all, since 7 - 3 = 4.
s: Europe and Asia joined as Eurasia
The two Americas joined as America
Africa joined with Eurasia; three joins in all

questions.q:
'Counting the continents is a matter of choice, not of measurement.' Analyse this statement using the chapter's four counts (four, five, six and seven continents).
(a) Which two continents appear, unchanged, in all four counts, and why do they never change?
(b) Name the three joins of adjoining landmasses that make the counts differ.
(c) In how many of the four counts is Africa a continent on its own?
(d) Suppose a new count joined North America with South America but kept every other continent of the seven-continent list separate. How many continents would it have, and does it match any of the chapter's four counts?
(e) Which count is used most, and does that make the others wrong? Judge.
questions.a: (a) Antarctica and Australia: neither is joined with any other landmass in any count. (b) North America with South America (America); Europe with Asia (Eurasia); Africa with Eurasia (Africa-Eurasia). (c) Three: the five-, six- and seven-continent counts. (d) Six (Africa, America, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe). It matches none of the four: the chapter's six-continent count keeps the Americas apart and joins Europe and Asia into Eurasia instead. (e) The seven-continent list is the most widely adopted, but the others are not wrong: each comes from grouping the same landmasses differently, so the number depends on our choice.
s: Part (a): Antarctica and Australia, never joined
Part (b): the three joins
Part (c): three counts
Part (d): six, matching none of the four counts (the book's six joins Europe-Asia, not the Americas)
Part (e): seven is most used; the others are choices, not errors

questions.q:
A geography club is painting a world wall for the junior classes, who use the standard textbook and atlas. Team X wants to paint Europe and Asia in one colour labelled 'Eurasia'. Team Y wants two colours labelled 'Europe' and 'Asia'.
(a) What does the map show about Europe and Asia as land?
(b) Why are they nevertheless generally counted as two?
(c) Who often treats them as one, and under what name?
(d) Which team's design suits this wall better? Justify using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) They form a single landmass. (b) For historical and cultural reasons, Europe's evolution has been very different from Asia's. (c) Geologists, who often call it 'Eurasia'. (d) Team Y: the juniors follow the most widely adopted list of seven continents, which shows Europe and Asia separately, so two colours match what they use.
s: Part (a): one single landmass
Part (b): different historical and cultural evolution
Part (c): geologists, as Eurasia
Part (d): Team Y, matching the widely used seven-continent list

questions.q: The five Olympic rings stand for five inhabited continents. Compared with the seven-continent list, which continent has no ring, and which two continents share one ring?
questions.a: Antarctica has none; North and South America share one
o: Antarctica has none; North and South America share one
Australia has none; Europe and Asia share one ring
Antarctica has none; Europe and Asia share one ring
Africa has none; North and South America share a single ring

questions.q:
Compare the chapter's five-continent count with the five continents represented by the Olympic rings, and analyse why two lists of 'five continents' can differ.
(a) Write both lists.
(b) Which continents appear in one list but not the other?
(c) Explain the difference over Europe and Asia.
(d) Explain the difference over Antarctica.
questions.a: (a) Five-continent count: Africa, America, Antarctica, Australia, Eurasia. Olympic rings: Africa, America, Asia, Australia, Europe. (b) Only in the count: Antarctica and Eurasia. Only in the rings: Asia and Europe. (c) The count joins Europe and Asia as the single landmass Eurasia; the rings keep them separate. (d) The rings were chosen to represent five inhabited continents, and Antarctica is not among them; every count in the chapter, including the five-continent count, lists Antarctica.
s: Part (a): both lists correct
Part (b): Antarctica and Eurasia versus Asia and Europe
Part (c): Eurasia joined in the count, separate in the rings
Part (d): rings stand for five inhabited continents without Antarctica; every count lists it

questions.q: A quiz answer sheet says: 'In the five-continent count, Africa is joined with Eurasia.' Which correction does the chapter support?
questions.a: Only the four-continent count joins them; the five keeps Africa apart
o: Only the four-continent count joins them; the five keeps Africa apart

o: A smaller piece of land with water on all sides

A piece of land with water on three sides only
Any stretch of land that lies along a sea coast

questions.q: True or False? 'Dakshin Gangotri is not the only base station India has set up in Antarctica.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The slip would be to read 'first' as 'only'. Dakshin Gangotri, set up in 1983, was India's first scientific base station there; two more bases were established later, so India has set up three.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: Dakshin Gangotri (1983) was the first; two more bases came later

questions.q:
A school exhibition has a timeline panel on India in Antarctica, but some labels are missing.
'Year ____: India begins exploring the ice continent.
1983: India's first scientific base station is set up.
Later: more base stations follow.'
(a) Which year belongs in the blank, and how many years later did the first base come?
(b) How many bases has India set up there in all?

questions.a: (a) 1981, when the Indian Antarctica Programme began; the first base, Dakshin Gangotri, came 1983 - 1981 = 2 years later. (b) 1 + 2 = 3 bases. (c) About 40 teams. (d) No. The chapter says the Indian Antarctica Programme has been exploring Antarctica since 1981; 1983 is only when the first scientific base station was set up, two years into that work. The panel should open with 1981.
s: Part (a): 1981, 2 years before the base
Part (b): 3 bases
Part (c): about 40 teams
Part (d): no; exploring began in 1981, and 1983 is the year of the first base

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Lakshadweep Islands lie in the Arabian Sea.

questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.q:

questions.a: (a) A smaller piece of land, surrounded by water on all sides, left out of the continents. (b) Continents are also surrounded by water, but they are so large that they are not considered islands; Australia is a continent.

questions.q: A map card reads: 'Greenland = India's largest states added together.' The number of states is missing; use the one the chapter gives. If those states average about 2 lakh square km each, Greenland's area is about ___ lakh square km.

questions.q:
