questions.q:
A poster says: 'India has only about 1,000 islands, and the whole planet has just a few thousand.'
(a) Correct both figures using the chapter.
(b) Using the chapter's figure for India, about how many times India's count is one lakh (1,00,000)? Round to the nearest whole number, and say whether the planet's real total is above or below one lakh.
questions.a: (a) India has more than 1,300 small islands, and the planet has lakhs of islands, not a few thousand. (b) 1,00,000 / 1,300 is about 76.9, so about 77 times; the planet's total is above one lakh, since 'lakhs' means more than one lakh.
s: Part (a): India more than 1,300; the planet lakhs
Part (b): about 77 times; the planet's total is above one lakh

questions.q: 'An island is not just any land with water around it.' Justify this statement using the chapter. Cover: what an island is; why a continent such as Australia is not an island; how much islands vary in size, with the chapter's largest example; and India's islands and their two major groups.
questions.a: An island is a smaller piece of land surrounded by water on all sides, left out when the continents are listed. Continents such as Australia are also surrounded by water, but they are so large that they are not considered islands. There are lakhs of islands of very different sizes: the largest, Greenland, equals the 10 largest states of India added together. India has more than 1,300 small islands, with two major groups: the Andaman and Nicobar Islands in the Bay of Bengal and the Lakshadweep Islands in the Arabian Sea. So size, not just the water around it, decides whether land is an island.
s: Island: a smaller piece of land with water on all sides
Continents are too large to be islands, though water surrounds them
Lakhs of islands of very different sizes; Greenland the largest
India: more than 1,300 islands; Andaman-Nicobar and Lakshadweep groups
Conclusion: size decides, not water alone

questions.q:
Read the statements about islands and Antarctica.
1. Continents are surrounded by water but are not counted as islands because of their size.
2. India has fewer than 1,000 islands.
3. India set up Dakshin Gangotri, its first base in Antarctica, in 1981.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 only
o: 1 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only

questions.q:
A sailor sets out from the coast of Kerala, sails west, and plans to visit both of India's major island groups.
(a) Which group does he reach in the sea he first sails into, and what is that sea?
(b) In which sea is the other group, and on which side of India does that sea lie?
(c) Does he have to leave one ocean for another to visit both groups? Explain.
questions.a: (a) The Lakshadweep Islands, in the Arabian Sea, which lies to the west of India. (b) The Andaman and Nicobar Islands are in the Bay of Bengal, which lies to the east of India. (c) No: the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal are both parts of the Indian Ocean, on either side of India.
s: Part (a): Lakshadweep, in the Arabian Sea (west of India)
Part (b): Andaman and Nicobar, in the Bay of Bengal (east of India)
Part (c): no, both seas are parts of the Indian Ocean

questions.q:
(a) What does the chapter say is left out when only the continents are listed?
(b) A student adds up the areas of all seven continents and says the total is all the land on the Earth. Is she right? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Smaller pieces of land surrounded by water on all sides, the islands, are left out; the continents do not include all landmass. (b) No: her total leaves out the islands (there are lakhs of them, of very different sizes), so the Earth's land is more than the continents' total.
s: Part (a): islands are left out of the continents
Part (b): no, the islands' land must be added

questions.q: A student says, 'An island must be tiny, like the small islands near India's coasts.' Which fact from the chapter shows her mistake?
questions.a: Islands vary in size; Greenland equals India's 10 largest states
o: Islands vary in size; Greenland equals India's 10 largest states
Islands vary in size; Australia is the largest island of all
All islands are tiny, but India has more than 1,300 of them
Islands are all large; only the continents can be really small pieces of land

questions.q:
In a quiz round called 'Island or not?', a team must judge four places: Greenland, Australia, the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, and Antarctica. All four have water on every side.
(a) Which two are islands or island groups, and which two are not?
(b) What rule from the chapter did you use?
(c) Which of the two islands or island groups lies in the Bay of Bengal?
(d) In a tie-breaker, Team 1 says Greenland should count as a continent because it is as big as India's 10 largest states put together; Team 2 says it is still an island. Which team wins the point? Justify using (a) and (b).
questions.a: (a) Islands: Greenland and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands; not islands: Australia and Antarctica. (b) Islands are smaller pieces of land surrounded by water; continents are also surrounded by water but are too large to be called islands. (c) The Andaman and Nicobar Islands. (d) Team 2: Greenland is very large, but it is the largest island, a piece of land left out of the continents; being big does not make it a continent, since continents are larger still and appear in the counts of continents, while Greenland does not.
s: Part (a): Greenland and Andaman-Nicobar islands; Australia and Antarctica not
Part (b): continents are too large to be islands
Part (c): the Andaman and Nicobar Islands
Part (d): Team 2; Greenland is the largest island, not a continent

questions.q:
(a) Greenland's area equals the 10 largest states of India added together. Is Greenland larger or smaller than India's largest state alone?
(b) Can we conclude from this that Greenland is larger than the whole of India? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Larger, since it equals that state plus nine more. (b) No: India is made up of all its states, not only these 10, so the whole of India is larger than its 10 largest states together, and so larger than Greenland.
s: Part (a): larger than the largest state
Part (b): no; India is all its states together, so it is more than its 10 largest states and so larger than Greenland (accept 'India is more than its 10 largest states')

questions.q: Write a three-line postcard from an Indian scientist at the settlement in Antarctica to her school. Each line must use a different fact from the chapter: one about the place, one about India's bases, one about life at the settlement.
questions.a: For example: 'Everything here is ice, and the cold is very harsh. Our first base, Dakshin Gangotri, was set up in 1983, and two more have been built since. Even so far away, our settlement has a library and a post office!'
s: Place: very cold, harsh, mostly ice
Bases: Dakshin Gangotri in 1983 and two more later
Life: a library and a post office

questions.q:
Analyse the Indian Antarctica Programme as the chapter describes it.
(a) When did it begin, and what kind of continent does it explore?
(b) What was set up in 1983, and what followed?
(c) How many teams have worked there, and on what?
(d) The chapter also says: 'Both oceans and continents play a vital role in shaping the climate of the Earth. They affect all aspects of life.' Using this sentence and your answer to (c), infer why the teams' research can matter to people in India too.
questions.a: (a) In 1981; Antarctica, a continent with a very cold climate and a harsh environment, mostly ice. (b) India's first scientific base station, Dakshin Gangotri; two more bases were established later. (c) About 40 teams of Indian scientists, especially on the evolution of climate and environment. (d) Inference from the two quoted facts: the teams study how climate and environment have evolved, and continents such as Antarctica help shape the Earth's climate, which affects all life, including people in India; so the research helps understand a climate that affects them.
s: Part (a): 1981; very cold, harsh, icy continent
Part (b): Dakshin Gangotri in 1983, two more bases later
Part (c): about 40 teams on climate and environment
Part (d): inference linking climate research to the quoted sentence

questions.q: A student argues that the Andaman and Nicobar Islands should be called a continent, since there are so many islands together. Which reply fits the chapter's meanings of the terms?
questions.a: They remain separate small pieces, not one continuous expanse
o: They remain separate small pieces, not one continuous expanse
They would be a continent if they lay in the Arabian Sea instead
They count as a continent only in the four-continent list
They are a continent because water surrounds them on all sides

questions.q:
A fishing village on India's coast keeps this record of its boats.
Year | Boats going out each day | Average catch per boat per day
2016 | 40 | 120 kg
2021 | 70 | 80 kg
2026 | 110 | 45 kg
(a) Work out the village's total catch per day in each of the three years.
(b) What happened to the total catch between 2021 and 2026, even though more boats went out?
(c) Which threat to the oceans named in the chapter does this pattern point to? Explain the term.
(d) A trader asks the panchayat to allow 30 more boats from next year. Should it agree? Decide using your answers.
questions.a: (a) 2016: 40 x 120 = 4,800 kg; 2021: 70 x 80 = 5,600 kg; 2026: 110 x 45 = 4,950 kg. (b) It fell from 5,600 kg to 4,950 kg, although boats rose from 70 to 110, and each boat's catch fell from 80 kg to 45 kg. (c) Overfishing: excessive fishing, which the chapter names as a cause of the decline of marine life. (d) No. Adding boats after 2021 already lowered the total catch, so 30 more would deepen the overfishing and the decline of fish; the panchayat should limit the boats instead.
s: Part (a): 4,800 kg, 5,600 kg and 4,950 kg
Part (b): total fell from 5,600 to 4,950 kg despite more boats
Part (c): overfishing, excessive fishing that reduces marine life
Part (d): no, more boats would worsen the decline; limit boats

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Without the oceans, there would be no rainfall on Earth.
Reason (R): The oceans send rain to the continents as part of the Earth's water cycle.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Old records of a port town describe ships carrying spices for sale, soldiers sent to attack a distant kingdom, and families moving to settle in a new land. Which uses of the oceans named in the chapter do these three show?
questions.a: Trade, military campaigns and migration
o: Trade, military campaigns and migration
Fishing, trade and military campaigns at sea
Migration, fishing and trade
Trade, migration and fishing

questions.q: True or False? 'The oceans matter only to the people who live along the coasts.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. The oceans send rain to the continents through the water cycle; the chapter says that without oceans there would be no rainfall and the Earth would be a desert, so people far inland depend on them too.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: oceans bring rain to the continents; without them the Earth would be a desert

questions.q: Arif says, 'Fishing is one of the oceans' blessings, but the same activity can also harm the oceans.' Is he right? Use the chapter.
questions.a: Yes. From early times people have used the oceans as a source of food through fishing. But overfishing, which is excessive fishing, is a cause of the decline of marine life, so too much of the same activity harms the oceans.
s: Verdict: right
Fishing has been a source of food since early times
Overfishing (excessive fishing) causes a decline of marine life

questions.q: A school holds a 7-day 'Ocean Week' that ends on the day the United Nations has set as World Oceans Day. The week begins on ___ June.
A folk-tale collector finds that almost every coastal community she visits tells stories of sea gods, sea monsters and treasures from the sea. What does the chapter say these tales reflect?
questions.a: The oceans' dangers as well as their blessings
o: The oceans' dangers as well as their blessings
Only the fear that people feel about storms and cyclones
Only the wealth that sea trade brought
A belief limited to India's own coasts

questions.q:
A coastal storyteller's tales include a sea goddess, a monster that sinks boats and a chest of pearls washed ashore.
(a) The chapter says such tales show the oceans' dangers 'but also their blessings'. Which item in these tales stands for a danger, and which for a blessing?
(b) Using what the chapter says elsewhere about the oceans, give one real danger and one real blessing that people living by the sea know.
questions.a: (a) Danger: the monster that sinks boats. Blessing: the chest of pearls, a treasure from the sea. (b) Danger: for example cyclones or tsunamis that damage coastal areas. Blessing: for example food through fishing, or trade by sea.
s: Part (a): the monster is a danger, the pearls a blessing
Part (b): one real ocean danger and one real blessing from the chapter

questions.q: 'It is our collective responsibility to protect the oceans for the future of the planet and of humanity.' Justify this statement using the chapter: what the oceans give everyone, and how human activity is harming them.
questions.a: What they give: more than half of the world's oxygen is produced by the oceans' flora, so they are called the planet's lungs; they send rain to the continents and regulate the climate; they are a major source of food (fishing) and medicine, as the World Oceans Day message says. Harm: people throw several million tonnes of plastic waste into the oceans every year, choking marine life; there are other forms of pollution too; overfishing causes the decline of marine life. Since everyone depends on the oceans and the harm comes from human activity, protecting them is everyone's responsibility.
s: Oceans' flora produce more than half the world's oxygen
They bring rain, regulate climate, and give food and medicine
Several million tonnes of plastic a year choke marine life
Overfishing and other pollution threaten marine life
Everyone benefits and humans cause the harm, so protection is collective

questions.q:
Read the statements about the oceans and life.
1. People began to use the seas for trade only in modern times.
2. More than three-fourths of the world's oxygen is produced by the oceans' flora.
3. Plastic waste thrown into the oceans chokes marine life.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 3 only
o: 3 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
2 only

questions.q:
In the photograph of the Earth from space, a student sees white shapes spread over the oceans and says they are floating ice.
(a) What are they, according to the chapter?
(b) How do they link the oceans to farms hundreds of kilometres inland?
questions.a: (a) Large masses of clouds. (b) Such clouds bring rain to the continents; the monsoon rains India expects every summer originate in the ocean, as part of the Earth's water cycle, and without such rains agriculture would suffer.
s: Part (a): large masses of clouds
Part (b): they bring ocean rain, such as the monsoon, to the continents and their farms

questions.q: A school far from the sea votes against joining an ocean clean-up campaign, saying, 'Looking after the oceans is the job of the coastal states.' Which reply is best supported by the chapter?
questions.a: Protecting the oceans is a collective duty, since all of us depend on their rain and oxygen
o: Protecting the oceans is a collective duty, since all of us depend on their rain and oxygen
The coastal states are right, since only the people who live by the sea and fish there are affected
Only the United Nations is responsible, since it set World Oceans Day
The oceans need no protection, since seawater keeps flowing across them and cleans itself

questions.q:
Read this message, given by the United Nations for World Oceans Day:
'...to remind us all of the major role the ocean plays in everyday life. It serves as the lungs of our planet, a major source of food and medicine and a critical part of the biosphere.'
A school far from the sea is making one poster for the day and has room to explain only one of the message's roles.
(a) Which fact in the chapter explains the phrase 'lungs of our planet'?
(b) Which use of the oceans from early times matches 'a major source of food', and which present-day threat does the chapter link to that use?
(c) Which human activity does the chapter say chokes marine life, and on what scale?
(d) The poster must choose between the 'lungs of our planet' role and the 'source of food and medicine' role, and must speak even to a student who never eats fish. Which role should it explain? Justify.
questions.a: (a) More than half of the world's oxygen is produced by the oceans' flora. (b) Fishing; overfishing (excessive fishing) is a cause of the decline of marine life. (c) Throwing plastic waste into the oceans, several million tonnes every year. (d) 'The lungs of our planet': the oxygen made by the oceans' flora is breathed by every student, inland or on the coast, whatever they eat, whereas the food role does not reach a student who never eats fish.
s: Part (a): ocean flora make more than half the world's oxygen
Part (b): fishing, and overfishing as its threat
Part (c): plastic waste, several million tonnes a year
Part (d): the lungs role, because everyone breathes the oxygen

questions.q:
The chapter concludes that the oceans 'play a crucial role in regulating the climate and sustaining life on Earth'. Riya explains this only with the oceans' oxygen; Sam explains it only with the rain they send.
(a) Is each of them using a fact the chapter gives? State both facts.
(b) Why does the conclusion need both facts together?
(c) Which of the two facts does the chapter use to say the Earth would be a desert without oceans?
questions.a: (a) Yes. Riya: more than half of the world's oxygen is produced by the oceans' flora, so they are called the planet's lungs. Sam: the oceans send rain to the continents as part of the water cycle. (b) Each covers only part: the conclusion is about both climate (the rain) and sustaining life (the oxygen as well as the rain). (c) The rain: without oceans there would be no rainfall, so the Earth would be a desert.
s: Part (a): both are chapter facts (oxygen from ocean flora; rain through the water cycle)
Part (b): the conclusion covers climate and life, so it needs both
Part (c): the rain fact; no oceans, no rain, a desert

questions.q:
A coastal museum shows three objects from a port town's past: a fishing net, a merchant's weighing scale and a sailor's helmet from a battle at sea.
(a) Which use of the oceans named in the chapter does each object stand for?
(b) Which one use from the chapter's list of four has no object here?
questions.a: (a) The fishing net: fishing as a source of food. The weighing scale: trade in all kinds of goods. The helmet: military campaigns. (b) Migration to other regions.
s: Part (a): fishing, trade and military campaigns
Part (b): migration

questions.q:
A student says, 'Trees on land make most of the oxygen we breathe, so harm to the oceans cannot affect our air.'
(a) By the chapter's figure, do land plants make more or less than half of the world's oxygen? Explain.
(b) Why would harming the oceans' plant life affect the air even of people far inland?
questions.a: (a) Less than half, since the oceans' flora produce more than half of the world's oxygen. (b) The oxygen made by ocean flora goes into the air everyone breathes, so harming it would cut more than half of the world's oxygen supply, which is why the oceans are called the planet's lungs.
s: Part (a): less than half, as ocean flora make more than half
Part (b): ocean oxygen is in everyone's air; the planet's lungs

questions.q:
A writer imagines a planet exactly like the Earth, except that it has no oceans at all. Its continents stand side by side with only dry ground between them.
(a) What would happen to rainfall on this planet, according to the chapter's reasoning?
(b) What would happen to the planet's oxygen supply, by the chapter's figure?
(c) Name two uses of the oceans in human history that the people of this planet could never have had.
(d) The writer must choose between two titles: 'A Desert World' and 'A Breathless World'. Which is better supported by (a) and (b)? Justify.
questions.a: (a) There would be no rainfall, since the oceans send rain to the continents as part of the water cycle. (b) It would lose the oxygen made by the oceans' flora, which on the Earth is more than half of the world's oxygen. (c) Any two of: migrating by sea to other regions, trading goods across the seas, sea-borne military campaigns, fishing. (d) 'A Desert World': with no rain the chapter says the Earth would be a desert, which is complete; the oxygen loss would be more than half but not all of it, so 'breathless' overstates.
s: Part (a): no rainfall, as oceans send rain through the water cycle
Part (b): loses more than half its oxygen, made by ocean flora
Part (c): two of migration, trade, military campaigns, fishing
Part (d): 'A Desert World', as no rain is complete while oxygen loss is partial

questions.q: Write a three-line poster for World Oceans Day at your school. Line 1 must give one way the oceans sustain life, line 2 one threat they face, and line 3 a call to act. Use only facts from the chapter.
questions.a: For example: 'The oceans' flora give us more than half of the oxygen we breathe. Every year we throw several million tonnes of plastic into them, choking marine life. Protecting them is all of our responsibility, so let us stop the plastic.' (Any correct chapter facts in the required order.)
s: Line 1: a correct way oceans sustain life
Line 2: a correct threat (plastic, other pollution, overfishing)
Line 3: a call to act linked to collective responsibility

questions.q: A class lists ways people have used the oceans since early times. Which item does NOT belong on the list, going by the chapter?
questions.a: Producing electricity from waves
o: Producing electricity from waves
Migrating to other regions of the world
Trading all kinds of goods
Conducting military campaigns

questions.q:
Compare how people used the oceans in early times with how human activity is affecting them today, and analyse what has changed in the relationship.
(a) Four uses of the oceans from early times
(b) One way the oceans shaped coastal cultures
(c) Two present-day harms, with the chapter's figure where it gives one
(d) What has changed in the relationship between people and the oceans
questions.a: (a) Migration, trade, military campaigns, and fishing for food. (b) Coastal people have tales and legends of sea gods and goddesses, monsters and treasures. (c) Several million tonnes of plastic waste thrown in every year, choking marine life (plus other pollution); overfishing, which causes a decline of marine life. (d) People once drew food, routes and culture from the oceans; now their activity, through pollution and overfishing, threatens the marine environment that gives them these things.
s: Part (a): migration, trade, military campaigns, fishing
Part (b): tales and legends about the sea
Part (c): plastic (several million tonnes a year) and overfishing
Part (d): from drawing benefits to threatening the marine environment

questions.q: A school beach clean-up removes 2 tonnes of plastic from the shore. Compared with what the chapter says people throw into the oceans every year, this is
questions.a: a tiny fraction of the several million tonnes thrown in yearly
o: a tiny fraction of the several million tonnes thrown in yearly
about half of the several million tonnes thrown in each year
about a quarter of the several million tonnes thrown in each year
about the same amount as people throw into the oceans in a whole year
